newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. probing staff in Rwanda war crimes tribunal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. probing staff in Rwanda war crimes tribunal.

text.p: As the Rwanda war crimes tribunal is about to hold its first trial, U.N. inspectors are investigating its administrative staff for hiring practices and other irregularities, according to reports on Wednesday.

Karl Paschke, the German diplomat, who serves as the U.N.'s inspector general, hinted at the investigation in a report Tuesday that concentrated on problems in procurement and poor planning in U.N. peacekeeping ventures.

But the New York Times and U.N. sources said on Wednesday that Paschke, the U.N. undersecretary-general for internal oversight services, had sent an investigator to Arusha, Tanzania, where the court is based, to look into complaints from its staff.

This would include allegations of victimisation of staff members, unexplained delays in procuring equipment and obstruction of efforts to publicise the genocide trials beginning on Thursday, the paper said.
In his published report, Paschke said that the tribunal, based in Arusha with an office in the Rwandan capital of Kigali, had hired staff that lacked expertise in some areas.

"The quality and strength of interpreters/translators were found to be deficient (and) the development of formal qualification criteria was needed for recruitment purposes," he said, adding that further administrative problems had surfaced that required an additional audit.

According to the Times, several staff members and legal experts on loan to the tribunal from European and other nations claimed that the acting chief of administration was slowing down if not sabotaging the work of legal officials of the court.

Non-African employees and experts attached to the tribunal contend they have been singled out for criticism in a campaign to drive them out of jobs, which are then filled through irregular channels as personal favours, the paper said.

On Thursday, Paul Akayesu, 43, will be the first defendant before the court, accused of genocide and crimes against humanity during the ethnic slaughter of more than half a million Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994, mainly by Hutu extremists.

Akayesu was bourgmestre, or local government leader, in Taba commune in western Rwanda during the genocide and is charged not only with failing to stop the killings, but inciting the public to slaughter, hunting down Tutsis and ordering killings.
The tribunal was created in November 1994. Its judges hoped the trials in Arusha would clearly show Africa that mass killings would not go unpunished.
So far 12 people are in detention and 21 indicted. But the trial cannot be videotaped or filmed because equipment is not in place, thereby preventing the trial from getting publicity.
With refugees from Rwanda fleeing bloodshed in Zaire, court officials are particularly anxious that people draw a lesson from the trial on mass genocide.
On the other hand the trial may not mean much to those carrying out new ethnic killings in chaotic eastern Zaire, nor to many of the Hutu refugees uprooted by fighting this month.
"I wish the tribunal all the best but it must be said that its timing is terrible, considering Zaire," said a U.N. official in Nairobi.
